title: Closing narration: Feather's assessment and the Sketches of Spain excerpt
summary: Johnston reads critic Leonard Feather's assessment and plays an excerpt from Sketches of Spain.

And a special harmonic evidenced by Duke Ellington has remained firmly rooted to jazz and as a consequence has succeeded in taking the music a step further along the path to orchestral maturity.

Six years later, in an article called 'The Individualism of Gil Evans' written for the Monterey Jazz Festival Bulletin, this is 1966, Feather says the basic value of Evans' contribution has always been his ability to weave new tone and textures sometimes out of familiar material, usually with unfamiliar instrumentations.

He has done more than any other writer to remove modern jazz from the strictly sectionalised reeds, brass, rhythm concept that dominated the swing era. Ellington and Strayhorn his only peers on this level have almost always operated within the familiar orchestral framework.
Evans has been able to experiment with groups of various sizes and shapes."

Now we are going to listen to a tantalizingly short excerpt from the Miles Davis "Sketches of Spain" album for which Gil Evans won the Grammy Award in 1960. And we are going to hear a portion of the Concerto De Aranjuez.
The recorder has obviously picked up a terrible flaw in this album. However, it can be its heard in/perfect condition on Columbia CS8271 if one buys a brand new one.
Given the peculiarities however, of the recording industry Miles Davis will benefit but Gil Evans will not. Arrangers simply work for established or agreed upon sums.
